title: CFA Alternatives 8: Putting alternatives into a portfolio - how much, and on what conditions
subtitle: The liquidity budget, unfunded commitments, and why the optimiser gives you the wrong answer
whyItMatters: This is the lesson that pulls everything you have learned into one real decision. And it contains the biggest trap in the whole topic: feed alternative-asset data into a standard portfolio optimiser and the model will almost always recommend an absurd weighting.
openingQuestion: Why does mean-variance optimisation typically recommend an unusually high weight in alternatives?
openingOptions: Because alternatives really should be a large share of the portfolio
Because the inputs are distorted: volatility and correlation look low
Because the model ignores the transaction costs of alternatives
Because alternatives have outperformed equities historically
explanation: An optimiser is extremely sensitive to its inputs, and it piles weight into whatever appears to have low risk and low correlation. Alternatives look that way not because they are, but because appraisal-based valuation smooths the return series - the same effect covered in lesson two. The result is that the model amplifies a measurement artefact into an allocation recommendation. The industry deals with this three ways: unsmooth the return series before feeding it in, cap the allocation using a liquidity constraint instead of letting the model choose, and test the output with scenario analysis rather than relying on variance alone.

summary.keyIdea: Portfolio optimisation is an amplifier of bias: feed it a return series whose volatility has been compressed and the output is always an over-allocation.
summary.commonMistake: Believing the optimal weight without checking the inputs. Garbage in, garbage out - and here the garbage looks very much like good data.

application.title: The pragmatic fix
application.message: Restate the volatility of the smoothed component before optimising, or simply set the allocation cap by judgement.

sections.text: The last question of the whole journey: how much to allocate to alternatives. The answer should not come from an optimiser - and the reason lies in the lesson on performance measurement.
Why the optimiser reaches the wrong conclusion

The model is extremely sensitive to its inputs, and it piles weight into precisely those assets that appear to combine low risk with low correlation. Alternatives look that way not because they are, but because appraisal valuation smooths the return series. The result is that the model amplifies a measurement artefact into an allocation recommendation, and that recommendation always leans towards more.

sections.label: Three fixes used in practice
sections.text: Unsmooth the return series before it goes into the model; cap the allocation with a liquidity constraint instead of letting the model choose; and test the result with scenario analysis rather than relying on variance alone.
Unfunded commitments - the hardest obligation of all

When you commit to a fund, the money does not move immediately: the fund calls capital gradually as it finds deals. So you carry an obligation of known size but unknown timing. What makes it dangerous is that it is procyclical: funds call hardest when markets are falling and opportunities are plentiful - exactly when the rest of your portfolio is losing value and liquidity is scarcest.

lines: Your allocation constraint should come from your own obligations.
Not from the output of a model fed on smoothed data.

diagram.label: Smoothing → reported volatility and correlation falsely low
The model piles weight into whatever looks least risky
A measurement artefact becomes an allocation recommendation
Fixes: unsmooth, cap on liquidity, run scenarios

realWorldExample.company: Unfunded commitments - the obligation that is not on the balance sheet
realWorldExample.description: Committing 100bn to a PE fund does not mean 100bn leaves the account today. The GP calls capital gradually over three to five years, at moments of their choosing. The investor therefore carries a payment obligation with no fixed date, and that obligation tends to be called hardest exactly when markets are falling - because that is when there are deals at good prices. Anyone who sizes their allocation on capital already drawn, forgetting the unfunded part, will discover a liquidity shortfall at the worst possible moment.

quiz.question: Why does an optimiser recommend too high a weight in alternatives?
options: Because the model cannot handle assets with a long lock-up
Because the model always favours whatever returned most historically
Because smoothed inputs make risk and correlation look too low
Because alternatives data has fewer observations than equities
quiz.explanation: The model is not wrong - it does its job faithfully on the data it is given. The problem is in the data, and optimisation amplifies the flaw rather than exposing it. A long lock-up is a constraint you have to impose by hand, and a short data history widens the confidence interval rather than pushing the weight up; neither explains why the recommended weight comes out systematically too high.

quiz.question: What kind of obligation does an unfunded commitment create?
options: An obligation to hold the fund interest for its whole life
An obligation to pay periodic interest on the undrawn part
An obligation to guarantee the fund's borrowings from banks
A payment obligation whose timing is unknown, decided by the GP
quiz.explanation: Not controlling the timing is what makes this obligation far harder to manage than a loan with a fixed repayment schedule. You pay no interest on undrawn commitments, you do not guarantee the fund's leverage, and while you do hold the interest for the fund's life, that is illiquidity rather than an obligation to pay - the defining feature here is a cash call you cannot put in a diary.

quiz.question: Why are commitments usually called hardest when markets are falling?
options: Because that is when the GP sees plenty of deals at good prices
Because rules force a fund to deploy fully when markets fall
Because other investors redeem, so the fund covers a shortfall
Because the fund's borrowing costs rise, so it needs equity
quiz.explanation: This is exactly what makes the investor's own liquidity risk and the fund's need for cash positively correlated at the worst possible moment. No rule compels a fund to deploy into a falling market - the GP does it because that is when assets are cheap. A closed-end private fund has no redeeming investors to cover, and higher borrowing costs change the deal structure rather than triggering a call.

quiz.question: What does a liquidity budget mean in allocating to alternatives?
options: Holding part of the portfolio in cash to cover the fund's management fees
Capping how much capital can be locked up, against known outflows
Investing only in funds that permit quarterly redemptions
Spreading capital evenly over years to reduce timing risk
quiz.explanation: This puts the constraint on the investor's own side of the balance sheet, rather than letting an optimiser decide how much capital gets locked away. Holding cash for fees is housekeeping, not a budget; restricting yourself to quarterly-liquid funds throws away the illiquidity premium entirely; and spreading commitments across vintages manages timing risk, which is a different problem from being able to meet a known payout.

quiz.question: Why does scenario analysis add something that variance analysis cannot?
options: Because it draws on a longer history and gives steadier estimates
Because it yields a single more precise figure for the optimal weight to hold
Because it asks 'what if this happens' instead of assuming a distribution
Because it removes the effect of appraisal smoothing altogether
quiz.explanation: Variance describes the day-to-day wobble; a scenario describes what happens in the tail - which is exactly where alternatives inflict their damage. Scenario analysis does not use more data, it uses less: it picks one specific state of the world. It produces no optimal weight at all, only a pass or a fail. And it does not undo smoothing, which has to be corrected in the return series itself.

keyTakeaways: Optimisation amplifies a measurement artefact into an allocation recommendation
Three fixes: unsmooth the returns, cap on liquidity, run scenarios
An unfunded commitment is an obligation with no fixed date
Commitments are called hardest when markets fall - exactly when you are short of liquidity
The constraint should come from the investor's obligations, not from the model's output

practicePrompt.question: A university endowment is obliged to spend 5% of assets each year. The model recommends a 45% allocation to alternatives. How should it respond?
options: Accept it, since the model optimised over a full historical record
Check the liquidity budget before raising the allocation at all
Cut it to 10%, because that is the usual industry allocation
Refuse outright, as alternatives are too risky for an endowment
practicePrompt.explanation: The 45% figure may be right or wrong, but you cannot settle it by comparing with an industry average or by a feeling about risk - which is what the other two options do. The decisive question is whether the endowment can still meet its known obligation in the worst case: markets down, no exits available, and the GPs calling capital hard at the same time.
